questions.q: Per this lesson, what does integration-focused questioning tend to target more than whether two systems can connect under ideal conditions?
options: The visual appearance of the integration diagram
What happens when the connection is slow, down, or inconsistent -- timeouts, partial failures, out-of-order data, and conflicting information
Whether the integration uses a popular, well-known vendor
How many total systems exist in the organization
questions.explain: Integration questioning is less interested in the easy, assumed happy path and much more interested in failure behavior -- what happens when a dependency is slow, unavailable, or returns conflicting data.

questions.q: What is the 'strong move' this lesson recommends when asked to reason live about synchronous versus asynchronous integration?
options: Picking whichever pattern is easiest to build and defending it as the only option
Refusing to answer since the choice is always arbitrary
Naming the actual business requirement that decides it, and considering a hybrid (synchronous with a short timeout, falling back to asynchronous) rather than treating it as a strict either/or
Always choosing synchronous regardless of the vendor's reliability
questions.explain: The strong answer ties the choice to the actual business requirement (e.g., staff needing a live answer during intake) while naming the tradeoff of full dependency on an external vendor's uptime, often landing on a reasoned hybrid rather than picking one pattern with no middle ground.

questions.q: What does idempotency protect against in the retry objection this lesson describes?
options: A retry accidentally causing a duplicate effect, such as submitting the same eligibility request twice
The eligibility API being slow to respond
Two legacy systems having different addresses for the same patient
A phased rollout missing its nine-month deadline
questions.explain: Idempotency specifically prevents a retried operation from causing a duplicate effect -- the objection asks what stops an automatic retry from submitting the same request twice, which an idempotency key addresses directly.

questions.q: In the rehearsed objection about two legacy systems disagreeing on a patient's address, what is a strong answer required to name, per this lesson?
options: A generic statement that 'data quality will be handled'
An explicit data-reconciliation rule for which source wins, with a named owner of that decision
A promise to delete one of the two legacy systems immediately
An unrelated security control
questions.explain: A strong answer names a specific, owned reconciliation rule for which source wins when two systems disagree -- a vague assurance that data quality will be 'handled' doesn't answer the specific conflict-resolution question being asked.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say 'we'll just call the API' is rarely a complete answer to an integration question?
options: Because calling the API is technically impossible in most designs
Because boards never ask about APIs at all
Because confirming the integration point exists is the easy, already-assumed part; what's actually being evaluated is the call's failure behavior, which that answer doesn't address
Because APIs should never be used in healthcare integrations
questions.explain: A board already assumes an API call would happen -- that's not what's being tested. What's evaluated is everything around the call: slowness, disagreement between sources, and outright failure, none of which 'we'll just call the API' addresses.
